title: Olives & Agave Brings the Levant to Santa Rosa
summary:
After 35 years of crepes, Maher Fakhouri opens Olives & Agave in Montgomery Village, a Mediterranean love letter to the flavors of home.

The post Olives & Agave Brings the Levant to Santa Rosa appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Nearly 20 years ago, on a trip home to Jordan, restaurateur Maher Fakhouri bought chicken shawarma from a street vendor and ate it on the sidewalk. Nothing fancy. Just seasoned chicken, garlicky sauce and pickles wrapped in warm flatbread — the kind of food best eaten with your hands and a few napkins nearby.

“It was so simple and delicious,” he recalled. “I had to share it when I came back.”

It took a few years to get the recipe right, but today, that shawarma is tucked into the sandwich section at Crepevine, Fakhouri’s Bay Area brunch chain. It’s an outlier among the Nutella crepes, eggs Benedict and omelets, but also one of the chain’s best sellers. That’s saying something for a restaurant with crepes in its name and 22 varieties on the menu.

But this isn’t a story about Crepevine. It’s about Fakhouri’s newest restaurant, Olives & Agave, in Santa Rosa’s Montgomery Village, just steps from Crepevine. The two restaurants share a general manager, Mond Noor, and a fondness for chicken shawarma.

At Olives & Agave, that simple sandwich is no longer an outlier. It’s part of a broader menu that draws on the cuisines of the Levant — including Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Israel and Lebanon — along with Mediterranean flavors from Spain and Greece to Turkey and Morocco.

For Fakhouri, the restaurant is personal: a chance to showcase the food of his childhood, his family’s traditions, and the recipes he’s carried with him for decades.

“This cuisine is not well represented here,” Fakhouri said of Sonoma County. That’s beginning to change, with a wave of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and Persian restaurants opening in the area. But musakhan and kibbeh aren’t exactly household words. Yet.

A long time coming

Fakhouri has spent a lifetime in the restaurant business, cooking almost everything except the food he grew up eating. At nearly 70, he was ready to change that.

The former Cascabel, which had been empty for more than a year, seemed the perfect spot. When the Montgomery Village landlord approached him, Fakhouri pitched a Mediterranean restaurant. He opened Olives & Agave in early October with Noor, a friend who serves as general manager, and his partner, Amal Dahdal, who runs the kitchen with an iron garlic press.

As we toured the space, I had to ask about the name. The olives were obvious. The agave, less so.

“Well, we sold a lot of tequila at Cascabel,” Fakhouri said, referring to the Mexican restaurant he helped launch in the same space. “And we use agave in some dishes.”

The new restaurant no longer has a full bar, and tequila drinks aren’t on the menu. The connection felt tenuous.

“I hate that story,” I said, suggesting that the name might instead nod to the agave plants that grow across the Middle East. It was a stretch, but plausible.

Fakhouri smiled.

“I like your idea better,” he said, glancing at Dahdal, who was already heading toward the kitchen, with better things to do than talk to a reporter.

Every dish that leaves the pass must meet her exacting standards. If it doesn’t, it doesn’t go to the table. The agave discussion could wait.

The picky one

On a busy Tuesday afternoon, Dahdal holds a small metal pan of kinafeh over a gas burner, turning it slowly so the shredded phyllo crisps evenly and the two kinds of cheese inside begin to melt. It looks like a good way to burn your fingers, but the sweet-savory dessert has to be just right. Only Dahdal seems to know exactly how to angle the pan to get it there.

Dahdal, who grew up in Syria, is Olives & Agave’s self-appointed quality-control department. Every plate must pass muster; every family recipe must taste as she remembers it. If something is missing, she fixes it on the spot.

“I’m the picky one,” she said, making it clear that although she and Fakhouri share recipes, she has the final say.

“Food is in my blood,” she said.

Dahdal never attended culinary school. Instead, she learned by cooking alongside other chefs, working with Fakhouri and traveling to explore different cuisines.

That attention to detail extends to the chicken shawarma, which is brined for 24 hours, dry-salted for another day, then marinated and grilled. It’s a more labor-intensive recipe than the simpler version at Crepevine. When Dahdal finally got it right, Noor jumped up and down in the kitchen.

She knew it would become a centerpiece of the Olives & Agave menu. Noor enthusiastically agreed.

Tastes like home

Fakhouri takes his spices seriously. In the prep kitchen, airtight containers of sumac, cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, cumin, coriander and Aleppo pepper line the shelves alongside blends such as za’atar and baharat, a Lebanese seven-spice mix. It’s an impressive collection, and one that gets plenty of use.

“We don’t buy anything ready,” Fakhouri said.

Whole spices are roasted and ground in-house, and sauces are made from scratch. “The flavors make all the difference.”

That commitment extends to packages of finely ground yellow spice he imports from Jordan, often tucked into family members’ suitcases. He keeps it out of sight and uses it sparingly. He isn’t sure what it’s called in English. The best we could come up with on Google was “winter spice.”

It’s the taste of home, he said.

For Dahdal and Fakhouri, that matters. The food should taste the way they remember it.

For Dahdal, home tastes like fried kibbeh. When she moved to the United States, she couldn’t find the bulgur wheat balls filled with beef or lamb, onions and spices. Think arancini or croquettes, and you’re close.

Growing up, she ate kibbeh with tabbouleh and a dollop of yogurt to cut the richness. That’s how she serves it at Olives & Agave, too. She’s also making sure the kitchen staff gets every detail right, from the seasoning to the crisp outer shell.

“I don’t want the food to change flavor,” she said.

For Fakhouri, home is mansaf: braised lamb shank smothered in jameed, a tangy fermented yogurt sauce. Jordan’s national dish is more than comfort food. It’s pride on a plate.

Noor, meanwhile, has a special fondness for musakhan.

But making people feel at home takes more than a good plate of lamb or crispy falafel. For Fakhouri, Dahdal and Noor, hospitality matters as much as what comes out of the kitchen.

“One of us is there from opening to close,” Fakhouri said. “Every minute of the operation.”

Now nearly 70, Fakhouri still works the floor alongside Noor, greeting guests and making sure everyone feels welcome. At a time when every dollar counts and dining out can feel like a luxury, an owner who genuinely cares whether you’re enjoying yourself can make the difference between an OK restaurant and one worth returning to.

The dining room has burled-wood tables, soft sofas for lounging and a popular covered patio. The expansive main dining room has a little less charm but can accommodate larger groups. Servers are trained to explain not just what’s in each dish, but its meaning and history.

“Our guests need to feel that they are treated like they are at home,” Fakhouri said.

Best bets and staff favorites

Fakhouri and Noor recommend ordering five or six plates to share, as is customary in much of the Middle East. Start with hot and cold maza, the Middle Eastern counterpart to tapas: small plates of dips, vegetables, savory pastries and other bites meant to be passed around the table. Add a few larger dishes, and you have a feast.

Maza trio, $19: Choose three dips from a lineup that includes hummus, smoky baba ghanoush (roasted eggplant), muhammara (roasted red peppers and walnuts), tangy labneh and cooling tzatziki. Served with warm pita, it’s an ideal way to start the meal.

Fried kibbeh, $17: One of Dahdal’s childhood favorites and a good introduction to Middle Eastern cooking. Order a plate for the table, though you may not feel particularly inclined to share.

Chicken shawarma wrap, $19: There’s no rushing this chicken, and the extra effort pays off. The deeply seasoned meat begs for a generous slather of the kitchen’s toum, a fluffy, unapologetically garlicky sauce.

Musakhan rolls, $16: Think Middle Eastern taquitos, filled with shredded chicken, onions, sumac and olive oil, then tucked into thin flatbread and crisped on the griddle. Noor remembers his mother baking bread three times a day over an open fire, drenching it in olive oil and piling it high with chicken. These rolls are the fun, handheld version.

Mansaf, $38: Tender lamb and rice smothered in tangy fermented-yogurt sauce, with almonds for crunch. This Jordanian comfort food is worth venturing beyond your usual order to try.

Falafel, $12: Made with chickpeas and fava beans, fresh herbs, garlic and an in-house blend of eight spices. These vegetarian favorites are fried to order, so there’s no excuse for a tepid, mushy version. Nobody here wants you to get a soggy falafel.

Zarzuela, $36: This Spanish-style seafood stew features fish, prawns and mussels in a tomato-based broth. Think of it as cioppino’s Mediterranean cousin, and save some bread to mop up the sauce. Dinner only.

Lamb shank tagine, $38: A whole lamb shank, tender enough to pull apart with a fork, served with spiced couscous studded with apricots. Fragrant spices and sweet fruit bring classic Moroccan flavors to the plate.

Kebabs, $25 to $28: Go for the mix-and-match skewers, ideally shish tawook (marinated chicken) and kafta (spiced ground meat). They’re tender and nicely charred. Drag them through the dips you ordered earlier — or order another round.

Kinafeh, $12: Fried cheese for dessert? Absolutely. This crispy shredded-phyllo pastry has a warm, melty cheese center and a drizzle of rosewater syrup. Sweet, salty and a must for first-timers.

Olives & Agave is at 909 Village Court, Montgomery Village, Santa Rosa. Open daily from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. 707-843-7365, olivesandagave.com

title: Little Saint Owners List Healdsburg Estate for $22 Million
summary:
Formerly part of actor Fred MacMurray's famed ranch, the 52-acre property on the Russian River includes charming interiors by acclaimed Bay Area designer Ken Fulk.

The post Little Saint Owners List Healdsburg Estate for $22 Million appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Jeff and Laurie Ubben, owners of Little Saint restaurant and music venue, have listed their 52-acre Healdsburg estate for sale. Dubbed Flax Estate and Vineyard, the property includes a main home, farmhouse, cottage, entertainment barn, Pinot Noir vineyard and direct access to the Russian River. The asking price is $22,000,000.

Once part of MacMurray Ranch, owned by late Hollywood actors Fred MacMurray and his wife June Haver, the estate now accommodates the Ubben family and their guests, including some of the musicians who have played the intimate venue at Little Saint. Musical acts such as Beck, boygenius and Rufus Wainwright have graced the stage at Healdsburg’s esteemed vegan restaurant.

The two-parcel property’s three residences have a total of 12 bedrooms, 14 bathrooms and 15,018 square feet of living space.

The main residence is a modern rectilinear dwelling with flat roofs, white walls inside and out with black steel-framed windows. Walls are alight with large windows and views in every room, including the hallway. Dramatic sculptural elements — like a striking MT (pronounced “empty”) circular chair on the patio, decorative spheres in the hallway and repeating brass accents in the lounge — enliven the clean-lined aesthetic.

Acclaimed San Francisco designer Ken Fulk designed the historic farmhouse and guesthouse interiors. The dwelling has all the Fulkian design surprises that launch his quaint cottage style into the playful stratosphere, achieving spaces that are both stunning and cozy. 

The farmhouse is painted a folksy barn red that, with minimal adornments, hits a decidedly modern note. The red is repeated in the striped upholstery of the poolside loungers. The transitional board-and-batten interior features cozy cottage decor, rich in pattern and layered with curiosities from vintage trophies to dog artwork. Unafraid of overstatement, Fulk chose bookshelf-mural wallpaper for the library’s walls.

One bathroom has gold honeybee wallpaper fittingly contrasted with black honeycomb shower tile. Another has chicken-motif wallpaper and marble arabesque tile with grout lines that suggest chicken wire.

The guesthouse kitchen has purple and gold-patterned tile repeated in the ochre cabinets and in the botanical artwork on the wall. The white home’s porch has a delightful choice of teal on the deck.

The entertainment barn has knotty-wood cladding on the inside, a chandelier over a large table and plenty of open space.

If Flax Estate’s design, dwellings, pool, river access and fertile land aren’t enough, there’s also a tennis court.

For more information on this property at 6697 Westside Road in Healdsburg, contact listing agents Alain-Martin Pierret, 707-696-9993, and Haley Skerrett, 707-483-8550; Compass Real Estate, 109 Mill St., Healdsburg. compass.com/homedetails/6677-6697-Westside-Rd-Healdsburg-CA-95448/2214743079676319225_lid

title: This Obscure Italian Wine From Sonocaia Estate Is Sonoma’s Best-Kept Secret
summary:
A former backyard vineyard developer showcases an uncommon Italian grape variety at his Sonoma winery.

The post This Obscure Italian Wine From Sonocaia Estate Is Sonoma’s Best-Kept Secret appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
There’s a reason you may not be familiar with Sagrantino, the signature red grape of the Umbrian hill town of Montefalco. Planted by only a handful of growers in California, the Italian variety accounts for just 20 to 40 acres of the state’s total wine grape tally. At Sonocaia Estate Winery in Sonoma, visitors can sample multiple vintages of Sonoma-grown Sagrantino wine.

The story

Ken Wornick spent decades developing backyard vineyards for wealthy homeowners in Silicon Valley until he found his true calling: growing a rare Italian grape variety for his own Sonoma County winery.

Wornick began his career as a geologist in San Francisco before founding Post & Trellis Vineyards in the late 1990s, at the height of the dot-com boom. The idea was simple, he says: Silicon Valley was minting millionaires by the dozen, so why not offer to plant vineyards to adorn the sites of their newly constructed mansions?

Though Wornick appreciated wine and understood geology, he had no idea how to develop a vineyard. Viticulture books guided him as he planted his first vines, and his client list grew.

After planting about 20 vineyards, Wornick decided to expand into winemaking. He bought an old building in Redwood City and founded La Honda Winery. Learning as he went, he began making wines for his Post & Trellis clients.

When a Silicon Valley venture capitalist offered to buy La Honda, Wornick and his wife Cynthia took the deal. They sold their home and the Post & Trellis business, then bought an 11-acre ranch in Sonoma. There, in 2016, he planted just under 2 acres of Sagrantino, inspired by an unforgettable wine he had tasted years earlier from Paolo Bea winery in Montefalco.

Though he had planted dozens of varieties for his vineyard clients over the years, Sagrantino was the grape that captured Wornick’s imagination. Dark and inky like Petite Sirah, yet with the velvety tannins of a Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon, Wornick says, “It had a magic for me.”

He produced his first vintage of Sonocaia Estate Sagrantino in 2021 and built a small-production winery on his home ranch in 2024. Wornick produces about 300 cases per year, from 100% organically grown estate fruit.

The vibe

Sonocaia is set on an 11-acre farm in Carneros that includes vegetable gardens, fruit and olive trees, chickens and an apiary for honeybees. Tastings typically take place at a long wooden table inside the neat, compact winery, among the tanks and barrels.

If you prefer an outdoor setting, there’s a large patio area, an offshoot of Wornick’s home, with a pool overlooking the vineyard. The feeling is friendly and intimate, like visiting a friend who happens to have a micro-winery in his yard and enjoys showing people around.

On the palate

Sagrantino is the star at Sonocaia. Though the grape is naturally bold and tannic, Wornick ensures the wines don’t overwhelm the palate. “I’m not interested in the hammer,” he says.

Tastings feature three bottled vintages from the Carneros estate: 2021, 2022 and 2023. The 2022 Estate Reserve Sagrantino ($65) is my favorite of the trio, with aromas of black fruits, spicy notes and a rich, velvety texture. All the bottlings are deep and inky, combining a big, tannic structure with silky elegance. These wines should be decanted for a few hours or stashed in the cellar.

You can also sample wines made on-site by Sonocaia’s assistant winemaker, Dominic Smith. Crafted from grapes grown in acclaimed Northern California vineyards, his Domesday Wine offerings include Grenache, Vermentino and a red blend.

Tastings cost $50 and are refundable with the purchase of a bottle.

Beyond the bottle

Sonoma County’s annual Black Cod Week, a celebration of the local fishing industry and the buttery fish also known as sablefish, is set for Oct. 17-25. Restaurants across the county are creating special dishes for the occasion, including Layla at MacArthur Place in Sonoma. Stop in for lunch and choose from black cod tacos or black cod with Manila clams in a miso-coconut milk broth.

Sonocaia Estate Winery, 20656 Hyde Road, Sonoma. Open by appointment only. sonocaia.com

Tina Caputo is a wine, food, and travel writer whose work has appeared in numerous publications, including SevenFifty Daily, Visit California, HuffPost, and Sonoma magazine. Follow Tina on Instagram @winebroad and view her website at tinacaputo.com.

title: Oakville Home Designed by Sea Ranch Architect Hits the Market
summary:
Designed by acclaimed Sea Ranch architect George Homsey, this Oakville home blends Spanish ranch style with distinct Northern California architecture.

The post Oakville Home Designed by Sea Ranch Architect Hits the Market appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
An Oakville home and two guesthouses on 45.2 hilltop acres, with views from Kalon Vineyard to Atlas Peak, is currently listed for sale. The work of a Sea Ranch architect, George Homsey, this circa-1993 home reflects the woodsy and relaxed Northern California architectural style known as Third Bay Tradition. With a total of six bedrooms, eight bathrooms and 9,262 square feet of overall living space, the asking price is $9,250,000.

Homsey was a founding partner of the San Francisco architectural firm EHDD. There, he worked alongside Joseph Esherick, Charles Moore and William Turnbull to create the iconic and celebrated style of The Sea Ranch. Homsey also designed San Francisco homes and even BART stations.

This Oakville home has the clay-tile gabled roof, sprawling footprint and plaster walls that typify a Spanish-style ranch home. The design seamlessly blends with elements that are distinct to Sea Ranch and Third Bay Tradition homes: knotty-pine clad interiors, asymmetrical shapes, high ceilings and window benches for a front-row seat to the outdoors.

The home’s design optimizes sunlight and views. A repeat of large windows showcases the natural setting while offering floods of light inside.

Mature landscaping surrounds the home — shrubs, climbing vines and a large lawn that receives dappled sunlight thanks to many oak trees. There’s a 51-foot infinity edge pool and a separate circular spa. There are several patios, some covered by a loggia that connect to the guesthouse. Further out is an olive grove and citrus orchard.

title: The Best Restaurants in Petaluma
summary:
From neighborhood favorites to exciting newcomers, these are the 22 best restaurants in Petaluma, chosen after dining our way through the city.

The post The Best Restaurants in Petaluma appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Petaluma has no shortage of good places to eat, from casual neighborhood favorites to ambitious fine dining. But which restaurants are really worth your time and money?

After eating our way through dozens of restaurants across the city, we’ve narrowed the field to the places we return to most often. Some are longtime favorites; others are newer arrivals that have quickly made their mark. Together, they offer a cross-section of Petaluma’s dining scene, from blistered Neapolitan pizza and handmade pasta to Korean comfort food, French bistro classics and elaborate tasting menus.

Here are our favorites — and what to order when you get there.

Old Caz

The pepperoni pizza may draw you into Caz Eats, the kitchen at Old Caz Backyard. But the Hot Pot pizza, topped with​ Sichuan peppercorns, maitake mushrooms, sausage, pickled chiles and kimchi, is reason enough to return.

Elijah Trujillo and Kayla Hendrix, former chefs with the Shokakko food truck, have built a beer-friendly menu that goes beyond the usual brewery fare. Slow-fermented pizzas share the menu with substantial salads and wood-fired vegetables, making this a destination for more than a pint and a slice.

20 Grey St., Petaluma, 707-347-5932, oldcaz.com/backyard

Bijou

Bijou makes a persuasive case for steak frites. The steak is tender, the peppercorn sauce rich, and the accompanying fries​ deliver the kind of straightforward pleasure that has made the French bistro classic endure.

The more casual sibling of Table Culture Provisions also excels at dishes meant for sharing, including delicata squash​ rings with onion dip, togarashi bacon cheese fries and Parker House rolls. On Mondays, a three-course dinner for locals​ costs $55. On Fridays and Saturdays, the kitchen stays open late, serving a menu of bites from 9 p.m. to 1 a.m.

190 Kentucky St., Petaluma, 707-753-9155, bijoupetaluma.com

L’Oro di Napoli

L’Oro di Napoli brought its Neapolitan-style pizzas to a larger Petaluma location in 2025, expanding on the formula that made its original Santa Rosa restaurant a favorite.

The pizzas have thin centers and charred, airy crusts that need little embellishment. The theatrical decor is part of the appeal. Mortadella hangs from a high-wire charcuterie display, while old movies play against the brick walls. It is dinner with a little spectacle.

The menu extends well beyond pizza, with antipasti such as fried calamari and Brussels sprouts with pecorino, along with fresh pasta, salads and entrees including zucchini Parmesan and branzino with lemon-wine sauce. The legendary lasagna, however, remains exclusive to the Santa Rosa restaurant.

208 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma, 707-981-7175, lorodinapolica.com

Cucina Paradiso

Sonoma County has no shortage of Italian restaurants, but Cucina Paradiso stands out for its warm service and straightforward approach to housemade pasta and desserts.

Best bets include pillowy gnocchi with Gorgonzola and walnuts, duck ravioli with sun-dried tomatoes and pine nuts, and the tiramisu.

This is the kind of neighborhood restaurant where you can settle in with a good bottle of wine and feel like a regular, even on your first visit.

114 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma, 707-782-1130, cucinaparadisopetaluma.com

Speakeasy

Speakeasy specializes in the kind of late-night eats that are more comforting than an old quilt.

Lobster macaroni and cheese, braised short ribs, cheesy patatas bravas, fried chicken and cheesecake anchor a menu designed for indulgence rather than restraint.

The restaurant is open from 5-10 p.m. Monday through Thursday and until midnight Friday and Saturday.

139 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma, 707-776-4631, speakeasypetaluma.com

Table Culture Provisions

Table Culture Provisions began quietly, appearing one or two nights a week at Wishbone in Petaluma.

Six years later, owners Stéphane Saint Louis and Steven Vargas have turned it into one of Sonoma County’s most sought-after dining destinations, with a multicourse tasting menu that has drawn comparisons to Michelin-level cooking.

From 4-6 p.m., the restaurant offers an à la carte menu of snacks and larger dishes, providing a more flexible way to explore the kitchen’s work.

Reservations are recommended.

312 Petaluma Blvd. S., Petaluma, 707-559-5739, tcprovision.com

Street Social

Owners Jevon Martin and Marjorie Pier spent years hosting pop-ups along the California coast before creating this small, deliberately personal dining room.

With six tables and 300 square feet of dining space, Street Social feels less like a conventional restaurant and more like an intimate dinner party.

At its busiest, the restaurant accommodates just over a dozen diners. That scale lends the experience a sense of discovery, as if you have stumbled upon a private culinary hideaway. And you have. But with a reservation, anyone is welcome.

29F Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma, 707-774-6185, streetsocial.social 

Quiote

Quiote is worth a special trip for its handmade blue corn tortillas alone. They provide the foundation for tacos filled with fresh rock cod, cochinita pibil with pickled onions, or al pastor with salsa verde.

The family-owned taqueria rewards diners who order beyond the basics. Add guacamole with serrano chiles, crisp raspadas or brothy Rancho Gordo beans. The Jalisco-style mole and braised chicken enchiladas are also worth trying.

121 Kentucky St., Petaluma. 707-774-6130, quiotemx.com

Stellina Pronto

Since opening in 2021, Stellina Pronto has cultivated a loyal following for its Italian pastries, baked goods and sandwiches. In May 2024, it added pizza to the mix, bringing together Neapolitan and New York influences.

The Margherita is a dependable classic. For something more substantial, try the Gianni, a white pizza topped with potato and garlic. The pastry case remains essential, particularly the cornetto, the Italian answer to the croissant.

23 Kentucky St., 707-789-9556, stellinapronto.com

Della Fattoria

Bread is the beating heart of Della Fattoria, the downtown bakery and cafe shaped by the late baker Kathleen Weber’s devotion to hearth-baked loaves.

The cafe puts those breads to work in avocado toast, French toast, hearty sandwiches and panzanella salad. The bakery case offers another reason to stop, whether for a pastry to eat on the spot or a loaf to take home.

143 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma, 707-763-0161, dellafattoria.com

Brigitte Bistro

At Brigitte Bistro, chef-owner Nick Ronan cooks the food he loves: hearty French bistro dishes like beef bourguignon, duck confit and steak frites, along with tableside beef tartare.

Ronan brings the flavors of his native France to Petaluma without sanding down their character for American tastes. His motto — “Love. Food. Wine. Passion. Life. People.” — serves as a useful description of the restaurant’s spirit.

841 Petaluma Blvd. North, Petaluma, brigittebistropetaluma.com

Soban

For traditional Korean cooking in Sonoma County, Soban is a reliable destination. Its menu includes dishes that can be difficult to find elsewhere in the region, from savory kimchi pancakes and japchae (glass noodles) to tteokbokki, the chewy rice cakes popular as Korean street food. Other standouts include spicy pork bulgogi, bibimbap served in a sizzling rice bowl and soft tofu soup.

255 N. McDowell Blvd., Petaluma, 707-769-3112, sobanpetaluma.com

Sarmentine

Sarmentine brought a taste of a beloved Santa Rosa French bakery to Petaluma in 2024. Its pastry cases are filled with cream-filled confections, chocolate croissants, brioche buns and fruit tarts. The passion fruit tart is a favorite. The Paris-Brest, made with pâte à choux and praline cream, and the mille-feuille are worth considering, too.

Small canelés, with their crisp exteriors and custardy centers, make our knees buckle with happiness. Recently, the bakery added traditional French crepes, including savory buckwheat galettes prepared by owner Alexandra Teulet, who studied the craft in Brittany.

840 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma, sarmentine.com

Central Market

At Central Market, chef Tony Najiola keeps a close eye on the dining room, checking each dish as it leaves the kitchen and making the rounds to see how diners are faring. His attention is reassuring rather than intrusive.

The open kitchen, bar and airy dining room put the cooking on display, but the food is the main attraction. Ingredients frequently come from Najiola’s Muleheart Farm, and the cooking reflects a commitment to letting them speak for themselves.

There are no elaborate culinary theatrics to distract from the essentials, just carefully prepared food with a clear sense of where it comes from.

42 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma, 707-778-9900, centralmarketpetaluma.com

Pearl

At Pearl, chefs and co-owners Brian Leitner and Annette Yang draw on the flavors of the Eastern Mediterranean and North Africa, with touches of Southern France and Spain.

The menu is built around bright, generous dishes: shakshuka, fresh pita, fattoush salad and braised meats, including brisket and lamb. A picnic plate of tabbouleh, hummus, labneh and warm pita offers a good introduction to the kitchen’s range.

500 First St., Petaluma, 707-559-5187, pearlpetaluma.com

Stockhome

Stockhome brings together Swedish staples and the Turkish and Middle Eastern street foods that have become popular in Sweden’s larger cities.

Swedish meatballs and pickled herring share space with lamb and beef kebabs served with garlic yogurt. The eggplant dip and grilled halloumi pita are also standouts.

The food is casual and family-friendly, with nods to California sensibilities. Consider it the United Nations of local dining.

220 Western Ave., Petaluma, 707-981-8511, stockhomerestaurant.com

Lunchette

Lunchette serves up big flavors in a small space. The downtown walk-up specializes in thoughtfully sourced lunch options that are fresh, satisfying and easy to take away.

The smoked trout salad, dressed with preserved lemon vinaigrette and served with roasted beets, pickled raisins and cashews, is a favorite. A warm grain bowl with roasted sweet potatoes and chickpeas offers a heartier alternative. Fresh pizza slices round out the menu for those wanting something more substantial to go with a salad.

25 Fourth St., Petaluma, 707-241-7443, lunchettepetaluma.com

The Shuckery

Oysters are a Sonoma County staple, but at The Shuckery they are the main show. The small, cozy restaurant serves excellent bivalves, including the delicate Kumamotos, our favorite. Try the Bingos: grilled oysters topped with cognac, mayonnaise, Parmesan and garlic. Plus, a full bar and outdoor seating.

100 Washington St., Petaluma, 707-981-7891, theshuckeryca.com

Brewsters Beer Garden

With 350 seats and an expansive outdoor setting in downtown Petaluma, Brewsters Beer Garden is an obvious gathering place for groups and families. The beer selection and relaxed atmosphere are reason enough to visit, but the kitchen offers more than the usual supporting cast. The menu includes smoked brisket, seasonal salads and our favorite buttermilk fried chicken sandwich (the secret: goat cheddar).

229 Water St. N., Petaluma, 707-981-8330, brewstersbeergarden.com

Wild Goat Bistro

Wild Goat Bistro, overlooking the Petaluma waterfront, pairs a casual setting with serious pizza. Its Neapolitan pies include the Fig and Pig, topped with four cheeses, prosciutto and fig spread. 6 Petaluma Blvd. N., Suite A5, Petaluma, 707-658-1156, wildgoatbistro.com

Seared

Seared brings the familiar pleasures of a downtown steakhouse to Petaluma, with rib-eyes, lobster macaroni and cheese enriched with bacon and Valley Ford Fontina, and prawns served with bacon fried rice and housemade kimchi.

The best value comes during happy hour, when substantial bites such as a prime rib dip, a mini wedge salad and macaroni and cheese are available for around $10 or less. The atmosphere is lively, making it better suited to a night out with friends than a quiet, romantic dinner.

170 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma, 707-762-5997, petalumaseared.com

Levant

Levant draws on the homestyle cooking of Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine in a welcoming restaurant in Petaluma’s Theater District.

Begin with warm pita and a sampler of hummus, smoky baba ghanoush, labneh and muhammara, a walnut-rich dip. From there, the menu offers fried halloumi, chicken shawarma and lamb dishes designed for the table. The food is generous and well suited to sharing, with plenty of reason to order another round of pita.

140 Second St., Suite 100, Petaluma, 707-658-8017, levantpetaluma.co

title: Sonoma County Wineries Offering Spontaneous Tastings and Social Hours

Remember when wine tasting was a spontaneous affair and you could pop in at just about any local winery that caught your fancy? The pandemic changed that. The good news is that many Sonoma County producers are moving away from strict “reservations-only” policies — welcoming walk-in visitors, hosting social hours and staying open later to serve the after-work crowd.

Here are the local wineries offering easy access to wine tasting experiences.

Walk-ins Welcome

Zin specialist Carol Shelton Wines in Santa Rosa invites walk-in tasters each day. Reserve flights cost just $20. 3354-B Coffey Lane, Santa Rosa. 707-575-3441, carolshelton.com

Comstock Wines, with a lineup that includes Zinfandel, Sauvignon Blanc and more, welcomes drop-by sippers to its Healdsburg estate with multiple flight options. 14210 Bacchus Landing Way and 1290 Dry Creek Road, Healdsburg. 707-723-3011, comstockwines.com

Swing by Montagne Russe in downtown Petaluma for cool-climate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay by the flight or glass. You can even bring along take-out eats from a neighboring restaurant. 155 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma. ​1-855-467-8773, russewines.com

Roche Winery & Vineyards accommodates drop-ins whenever possible at both of its Sonoma locations, making it a solid bet when you’re in the mood for a splash of Carneros Pinot Noir or Chardonnay. 22097A Bonness Road and 122 W. Spain St., Sonoma. 707-935-7115, rochewinery.com

Smith Story Wines in Healdsburg encourages visits from spontaneous types at its Bacchus Landing tasting room. Taste their eclectic lineup of wines, then stroll over to Dot Wine and see if they can squeeze you in. 14210 Bacchus Landing Way, Suite 200, Healdsburg. 707-494-5575, smithstorywines.com

Social Butterflies + Night Owls

Benovia Winery hosts happy hour from 4:30-7 p.m. on the fourth Thursday of each month. The Santa Rosa winery pours wines by the glass and serves complimentary snacks. 3339 Hartman Road, Santa Rosa. 707-921-1040, benoviawinery.com

On the third Thursday of each month, Dutton-Goldfield Winery in Sebastopol invites guests to pop in from 4:30-7:30 p.m. for happy-hour pricing on wines by the glass, and free snacks. 3100 Gravenstein Highway N., Sebastopol. 707-823-3887, duttongoldfield.com

title: Sonoma County Wineries Building a Brighter Future
summary:
In the face of an industry slump, Sonoma County wineries are focusing on accessible tastings, unique experiences and wines made for the moment.

The post Sonoma County Wineries Building a Brighter Future appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
By now, practically everyone has heard about the downturn in the U.S. wine industry. Not enough demand. Too much wine. Competition from other beverages. Younger generations opting out. Older generations aging out.

According to the 2026 BMO Market Report from BMO Bank, volume sales of U.S. wines declined 4% in 2025 for the second year running. Meanwhile, total market value rose 3% — with some of that growth attributed to higher bottle prices. Yet there are also some promising signs of stabilization. Tasting room visitation is still declining, but at a slower rate. Wine Business Monthly’s 2026 Tasting Room Survey shows an 8% dip in visits to Sonoma County wineries last year, and while that may sound dire, it’s a significant improvement from a 14% drop the previous year.

“I think there’s so much chatter around, ‘The market is hard, the industry’s down,’” says winemaker Sam Bilbro, the managing partner at Overshine Collective in Healdsburg. “I’m not going to deny any of that, but I know so many people who are seeing positive change — and not just young, different brands. I know some classic brands that are digging in and working hard.”

While some see an existential crisis, nimble Sonoma County vintners are working to build a future worth getting excited about.

One important way wineries are evolving to meet the moment is by making the world of wine more accessible — especially for younger generations. Increasingly, local producers are moving away from reservations-only policies to allow visitors more spontaneity. Others, such as Anaba Wines in Sonoma and DeLoach Vineyards in Santa Rosa, are lowering tasting fees and offering free wine flights during certain hours. Winery experiences are expanding beyond formal guided tastings to include immersive activities and casual visits that encourage social connection.

Bilbro points out that each of the wines in the Overshine Collective — including Overshine Wines, Idlewild, Comunità, Martha Stoumen, Reeve, and BloodRoot wineries — has its own approach to hospitality. But overall, he says, “Embracing fun helps. You can have great wine, but you can still just be sitting with a great view and listening to some loud soul music and having a good time. It doesn’t need to be stuffy in any way.”

At Idlewild, Bilbro says, the winery has shifted from offering high-end dinners to hosting more laid-back gatherings. On Fridays during the summer, Idlewild collaborates with Healdsburg’s Downtown Bakery & Creamery to offer wood-fired pizzas and wines by the glass and hosts art nights every couple of Wednesdays. “These events are never going to be what makes money for us,” says Bilbro. “It’s just about community. I think sometimes [wineries] are looking at it as, ‘Where’s my profit?’ Your profit comes when you have created the culture and then that starts to sustain you.”

Wineries are also staying open later and hosting pop-up events outside of Wine Country. “Especially for the younger consumers, they’re so hungry to have these connections and to be able to meet these winemakers face-to-face,” says Alex Sarovich, the founder of Own Rooted Hospitality. “But it’s really cost prohibitive to be driving up or staying the night in Wine Country if you’re based in San Francisco or Sacramento.”

Dancing Wines regularly hosts events in New York, Connecticut, and Los Angeles. Lauren Russell, who co-founded the Healdsburg-based winery with her mother Cynthia Russell, points out that the winery doesn’t have a tasting room, so its Dance Club gatherings are a way to meet consumers where they are. One of Dancing’s signature events is the Sip & Scent experience, which incorporates the winery’s line of vineyard-inspired fragrances into a wine tasting session.

“We’re doing all sorts of events, whether they’re interactive pizza-making classes or pop-ups at wine bars,” Russell says. “We’re inviting people in to just have fun and be playful with the wine.”

That approach extends to Dancing’s labels and language. Rather than listing a dozen aromas and flavors in a particular wine, the winery website opts for descriptions such as “juicy, like the best conversations” and “dark and playful as a midnight swim.” When Dancing was nearing its launch in 2023, its landing page led with the phrase, “You can’t taste wine when your mouth is full of adjectives.”

“There were all these adjectives falling around everywhere on the page and they were super-jumbled,” Russell says. “It was a visual representation of the fact that people get super-hung up in articulating the right tasting notes or finding the right ways to describe wine. A lot of that feels like a foreign language and that can be super-intimidating.”

High prices can be equally off-putting. During the pandemic, “premiumization” was an industry buzzword as home-bound consumers upgraded to higher-end wines. These days, with prices rising for everything from groceries to gas, people are looking for values.

“One of our goals at Overshine is, yes, we have $75 Pinot,” says Bilbro. “But we adamantly want to make sure we have wines priced in the low $30s so anybody can walk out of here with at least one bottle.”

Winemaker Pax Mahle, the founder of Pax Wines in Sebastopol, offers $25 wines in addition to pricier, single-vineyard selections. Originally created for restaurant by-the-glass programs, the Helios Chenin Blanc and Cuvée Syrah have sold thousands of cases. Mahle says he plans to add a Sauvignon Blanc next year. Though the winemaker says he has no plans to discontinue his signature wines, he might reduce production slightly so he can dedicate some barrels to his popular lower-tier wines. “I always tell my customers that for every $75 bottle of Syrah I drink,” Mahle says, “I probably drink 10 bottles of $25 crispy white wine.”

As consumer tastes evolve and the climate warms, Sonoma County wineries are exploring under-the-radar grape varieties to complement the region’s signature Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Winemaker Eric Prahl of Centennial Mountain in Healdsburg says Italian varieties grow particularly well in Sonoma County because of the region’s Mediterranean climate. Prahl has noticed a big spike in the popularity of Italian-style wines such as Carricante and Nerello Mascalese. This applies not only to consumers, but to other producers. “A lot of wineries — people you wouldn’t expect — are asking us for budwood,” he says.

Though he attributes part of their interest to a shift in consumer preferences toward brighter, more acidic wines, Prahl says it’s also a response to climate change. “Wineries are realizing that it’s getting harder and harder to grow [some of the traditional grapes] and make the same wines as 20 years ago.”

Bilbro, who focuses on Italian varieties at Idlewild and Comunità, says winemakers are paying more attention to what works best for a particular site or region. “By no means am I trying to say we shouldn’t be growing Cabernet, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay,” Bilbro says. “But it’s kind of crazy that you would plant a new vineyard and not even think, ‘Well, what is this exactly like in Europe?’”

Another benefit to offering wines made from less-common grape varieties, Sarovich adds, is that they are often made in a fresher style that attracts younger consumers and allows wineries to sell them at more affordable prices. “Stylistically, they’re often not being put in oak,” she says. “They’re not being aged for a long time. They’re being harvested earlier to craft wines that are lower in alcohol. You know you’re going to be selling this at a lower price point, so you’re not spending that money on the barrels.”

Newer wineries aren’t the only ones branching out. In recent years, established producers such as Kokomo Winery in Dry Creek Valley have expanded their portfolios to include new styles. Founder Erik Miller launched his Breaking Bread label in 2018. Made from certified-organic grapes, the line includes a Zinfandel pet-nat, orange wine, and a chillable red blend. The intent, he says, was to create something entirely new — not just a cheaper version of Kokomo.

“I was intrigued by the natural category,” he says, “and making a different style of wines using ancient techniques.” Miller says having both a traditional and a natural brand has helped increase his access in the distribution world. And as a bonus, Breaking Bread has brought new — and younger — customers to the Kokomo winery.

Though strategies vary, the common thread among the most resilient wineries, says Bilbro, is a willingness to put in the effort. “It’s harder right now. That’s undeniable,” he says. “But it’s not like there aren’t people coming here and it’s not like there aren’t people buying wine. I think for a long time we had it really easy and we don’t have it easy now. So, the question for most people in the industry is, is it worth the work?”

For many Sonoma County vintners, the answer is a resounding yes.

Hello, B.Y.O.!

Restaurants with Free Corkage Nights

Lately, it seems like restaurant wine pricing has gone through the roof. Why pay $18 for a single glass when you can bring your own bottle of Sonoma County wine and skip the corkage fee? Here are some of our favorite dining spots for BYOB deals.

It’s hard to beat locals night at Baked on the River in Guerneville. On Thursdays, comfort food fans get a three-course dinner for $25 and free corkage.

Petaluma’s Central Market is the place to be on Tuesdays, when the farm-to-fork restaurant offers complimentary corkage and 40% off wines by the bottle.

Every Monday, pay zero corkage and enjoy classic French fare in a romantic setting at La Gare French Restaurant in Santa Rosa.

Head for Glen Ellen Star every Wednesday for Neighborhood Night. That’s when diners can score two fresh and fabulous courses for $49, along with complimentary corkage.

Chef Charlie Palmer’s Dry Creek Kitchen and Folia Kitchen in Healdsburg waive the corkage fee for the first two bottles of BYO Sonoma County wines.

On Mondays, Stella offers free corkage on unlimited bottles to enjoy with the Kenwood restaurant’s exquisite, housemade pastas.

Sonoma Wine Shop & La Bodega, a homey Sebastopol hub for elevated plant-based cuisine, never charges a corkage fee for diners who bring in a bottle from the on-site wine shop.

At The Madrona, known for its epic burger and gorgeous salads, corkage is on the house during lunch service Wednesday through Friday.

Glen Ellen’s Poppy doesn’t technically offer free corkage, but the weeknight family-style meal is the next best thing. Get three courses, including wine, for $65 on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays.

Sugo Trattoria is a Petaluma go-to for fresh Italian food. It’s even more popular on Mondays, when diners can bring their own wine with zero corkage.

Easy Access

Spontaneous tastings and social hours

Remember when wine tasting was a spontaneous affair and you could pop in at just about any local winery that caught your fancy? The pandemic changed that. The good news is that many Sonoma County producers are moving away from strict “reservations-only” policies — welcoming walk-in visitors, hosting social hours, and staying open later to serve the after-work crowd.

Zin specialist Carol Shelton Wines in Santa Rosa invites walk-in tasters each day. Reserve flights cost just $20.

Comstock Wines, with a lineup that includes Zinfandel, Sauvignon Blanc and more, welcomes drop-by sippers to its Healdsburg estate with multiple flight options.

Swing by Montagne Russe in downtown Petaluma for cool-climate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay by the flight or glass. You can even bring along take-out eats from a neighboring restaurant.

Roche Winery & Vineyards accommodates drop-ins whenever possible at both of its Sonoma locations, making it a solid bet when you’re in the mood for a splash of Carneros Pinot Noir or Chardonnay.

Healdsburg’s BloodRoot Wines stays open until 7 p.m. daily, so it’s a great place to swing by after work for a glass of wine and some chill vibes.

On the third Thursday of each month, Dutton-Goldfield Winery in Sebastopol invites guests to pop in from 4:30-7:30 p.m. for happy-hour pricing on wines by the glass, and free snacks.

The Windsor tasting room for J. Cage Cellars stays open until 8 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays, and offers happy-hour specials on Thursdays and Fridays.

Martha Stoumen Wines in Healdsburg stays open until 7 p.m. Wednesdays, Thursdays, and Sundays, and until 9 p.m. Fridays and Saturdays. Walk-ins are welcome.

Alter Egos

Traditional brands show their adventurous side

Newer wineries with a natural bent aren’t the only ones fermenting outside the box. Long-established producers are also branching out, and some have even launched adventurous side brands. The idea is to give winemakers a chance to have fun and experiment while offering consumers — especially younger ones — a variety of wine styles to explore. Here are three “dual-personality” wineries worth discovering.

Kokomo Winery/Breaking Bread

Winemaker Erik Miller founded his Healdsburg winery in 2004 and built a reputation for producing terrific Dry Creek Zinfandel, Alexander Valley Cabernet Sauvignon, and a delicious rosé. Then, in 2018, he introduced Breaking Bread. Made in a lighter, lower-alcohol style than the Kokomo offerings, the lineup includes Zinfandel-based pet-nat and rosé, along with an orange wine, a whole cluster Pinot Noir, and Al Dente, a chillable Mourvèdre blend. Taste them at the Kokomo tasting room in Healdsburg.

Stewart Cellars/Guthrie Family Wines

When he’s not making serious, terroir-driven wines for Yountville-based Stewart Cellars — founded in 2000 by his father-in-law Michael Stewart — Blair Guthrie makes his own brand of wines at Guthrie Family Cellars in Sonoma. Guthrie takes a minimalist approach, starting with organically and biodynamically farmed grapes. Flavor profiles are bright and fresh, shining a spotlight on varieties such as Vermentino, Grenache Blanc, and Gamay Noir.

Obsidian Ridge/Rabbit Hole

Brothers Arpad and Peter Molnar launched Obsidian Ridge, their Lake County-based Cabernet Sauvignon brand, in 2002. Then, in 2020, they went down a rabbit hole. The Rabbit Hole line is a little on the wild side, taking an experimental, natural-leaning path. Current releases include a sparkling Pinot Noir pet-nat called Pezsgő, the Máslás red piquette, and a sweet white vermouth. Taste the wines at Obsidian Ridge Base Camp in downtown Sonoma.

Something Different

Not your typical tastings

Wine tasting is no longer just about wine. In recent years, local vintners have gotten wildly creative, putting their own personal stamp on winery experiences from unexpected food pairings to — well, anything goes.

The KC Lab x Hot Drops Challenge at Kivelstadt Cellars is bringing the heat with a taste-if-you-dare examination of wine’s interaction with spice. Taste playful wines with four different locally handcrafted hot sauces, sprinkled on crispy chicken bites.

Empanada pairings — a nod to the Keller family’s Mexican heritage — are a highlight of Keller Estate’s Terroir Experience. The winery also hosts epic Día de los Muertos gatherings and is planning a holiday posada.

Wine tasting is much more zen after a forest bathing session at Bartholomew Estate in Sonoma, led by a certified nature therapy guide. The estate also offers horseback riding.

The Donum Collection’s Art Tour is a self-guided, open-air meander through the winery’s collection of contemporary sculptures, scattered throughout the 200-acre estate. It includes 70 massive works by world-famous artists.

Anaba Wines invites guests to dink while they drink with Pickleball & Wine Tasting. You’ll play on Sonoma Wine Country’s most scenic court, overlooking Anaba’s Picpoul Blanc vineyard.

During the Hawley Winery & Vineyards Falconry Experience, visitors learn how majestic raptors protect grapes from voracious birds during the growing season. After touring the Dry Creek Valley vineyard estate you’ll sample current releases.

More Sips, Less Splurge

Budget-friendly bottles and tastings

Visiting wineries and purchasing bottles at retail can sometimes be spendy, but the trend appears to be shifting.

According to Silicon Valley Bank’s 2026 Direct-to-Consumer Wine Report, the average price for a bottle of Sonoma County wine among participating producers decreased more than 7% last year.

Pax Mahle of Pax Wines in Sebastopol says he is able to keep prices down for certain wines — such as his $25 Helios Chenin Blanc — by sourcing high-quality fruit from regions like the Sierra Foothills and Mendocino County, foregoing expensive new French oak barrels for large neutral casks, and opting for less-costly lightweight bottles sealed with screwcaps.

“The idea,” Mahle says, “is to make the best wine possible for the price.”

Tasting room fees are also becoming more affordable. Nearly a third of Sonoma County respondents to the Silicon Valley Bank survey reported lowering their tasting fees last year to boost visitation, and many have added entry-level flights at affordable prices. Some are even hosting free tastings on weekdays.

Here’s where to find some of Sonoma County’s best wine values — by the taste and by the bottle.

Values by the Bottle

Healdsburg’s Leo Steen Wines produces minimal-intervention, lower-alcohol wines at friendly prices. The fruity and floral Red Field Blend from Redwood Valley and organic Rose Ranch Sonoma Valley Rosé are gems at $25 each.

At Pax Wines in Sebastopol, bottle prices start at $25 for Helios Chenin Blanc and Cuvée Syrah and many offerings hover in the $30 range. Look for the zesty Springline Sauvignon Blanc ($30) and carbonic Alpine Peak Gamay Noir ($38).

Monte Rio Cellars in Monte Rio offers a whole lineup of interesting and delicious wines for $25 per bottle. Try the minerally Cemetery Road Alta Mesa Sauvignon Blanc or cherry-kissed Rivers Edge Lodi Sangiovese.

Pedroncelli Winery in Geyserville consistently offers lots of tasty bang for the buck. The citrusy Giovanni & Giulia Sauvignon Blanc, jammy Mother Clone Zinfandel, and structured Brother’s Mark Cabernet Sauvignon are all priced in the mid-$20s.

Free and Low-Cost Tastings

Pinot Noir specialist Anaba Wines in Sonoma just lowered the price of its classic Elements Flight from $45 to $25, available for reservations booked Tuesday through Thursday before noon.

Tastings of expressive cool-climate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are always complimentary at Bohème Wines in Occidental, so why not pick up an extra bottle while you’re there?

On Thursdays and Mondays from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., the bar tasting of Russian River Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and Zinfandel at DeLoach Vineyards in Santa Rosa costs $0. That’s right; it’s free.

Through November, Wine Road’s Sip into the Weekend program offers free tastings every Thursday and/or Friday. The deal applies at more than two dozen wineries in the Alexander, Dry Creek, and Russian River valleys.

The shared tasting room for Idlewild Wines and Comunità in Healdsburg presents low-key tastings of Italian-inspired wines for $30. For an extra 20 bucks, add a plate of imported cheeses, salumi and conservas.

Unti Vineyards pours flights of terrific Italian- and Rhone-style wines at its Healdsburg estate for just $25, year ’round.

The Taste of K-J flight at Kendall-Jackson Wine Estate & Gardens in Santa Rosa offers a mini snapshot of signature wines for $20. Both K-J and its sister property, La Crema in Windsor, host free tastings during Social Hour, held Thursdays from 3-6 p.m. until Oct. 29. No reservations needed.

title: The Best Desserts in Sonoma County, According to Our Food Team
summary:
Oct. 14 is National Dessert Day, so now would be as good a time as any to get acquainted with the best desserts in Sonoma County.

The post The Best Desserts in Sonoma County, According to Our Food Team appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Eat dessert first, because those peas and carrots aren’t going anywhere. No matter what mom said, we’re all about enjoying the sweeter things in life and worrying about the rest tomorrow.

National Dessert Day is Oct. 14, so now would be as good a time as any to get acquainted with the best desserts in the county. Read with caution, because this list is jam-packed with chocolate, sugar, whipped cream and cookies.

Story by Sofia Englund, Jennifer Graue, Heather Irwin and Maci Martell.

Heather’s Picks

St. Honoré Tart, Bijou

It’s exceedingly rare to see restaurant desserts created with the same finesse and artistry as the preceding meal. Bijou’s executive pastry chef, Sylvain Parsy, creates stunning masterpieces of sugar, butter and cream that make you forget about the calories and just embrace the magic. The St. Honoré Tart is made with gold-leaf-adorned almond and caramel chou and a pastry tart filled with cream. You really can’t go wrong with any of Parsy’s often-changing desserts, so don’t panic if the tart isn’t available. 190 Kentucky St., Petaluma, 707-753-9155, restaurantbijou.com

Soft Serve, Valley Ford Creamery

What started as an afterthought during a visit to this Valley Ford cheese factory and cafe has haunted my dreams — a swirling cone of creamy soft serve from local Jersey cows. The smooth, gelato-like texture is worth the trip. 14390 Valley Ford Road, Valley Ford, 707- 875-0703, valleyfordcheese.com

Semisweet Chocolate Chip Cookie, Sebastopol Cookie Company

It’s all about the cookies at this hole-in-the-wall bakery. Fresh chocolate chip cookies are outstanding on their own, but in the summer, they add an ice cream middle. Just like milk and cookies, but better. 168 N. Main St., Sebastopol. 707-824-4040, sebastopolcookiecompany.com

Choux au Craquelin, Poppy

We all have that extra dessert pocket in our stomachs, right? No matter how much delicious bread, butter and cream you’ve already eaten, make way for this baseball-sized puff filled nearly to bursting with velvety espresso mousse. 13690 Arnold Drive, Glen Ellen, 707-938-2130, poppyglenellen.com

Tiramisu, Portico

Feel free to dive into a hefty slice of this espresso-soaked dessert made with mascarpone rather than whipped cream. The sweetness is toned down, making it a calorie-worthy dessert without the sugar shock. 100 N. Main St., Sebastopol, 707-888-9136, porticosocialfood.com

Baked Gelaska, Stella

This one’s a true showstopper. Stella’s “Baked Gelaska” is a riff on baked Alaska, with sponge cake, raspberry sorbet and vanilla gelato topped with a swirl of torched marshmallow fluff. 9049 Sonoma Highway, Kenwood, 707-801-8043, stellakenwood.com

Strudel, Tisza Bistro

This seemingly simple dessert is made in-house by stretching the dough into thin, buttery layers filled with seasonal fruit, including apples, cherries and poppy seeds. 165 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg, 707-291-5193, tiszabistro.com

Friday Pie Day, Hazel

Every Friday is pie day at this Occidental restaurant. Co-owner Michele Wimborough’s pies are legendary, ranging from peanut butter and blackberry to Dutch apple and lemon meringue. You never know what she’ll be making, which is half the fun of your pie adventure. Pies typically last through the weekend. 3688 Bohemian Highway, Occidental, 707-874-6003, restauranthazel.com

Sofia’s Picks

Glacée and Petit Beurre Cookies, Goguette Bread

Warm Sonoma County nights make for a perfect excuse to indulge in this popular boulangerie’s housemade glacée — a decadent French custard-style ice cream — to the tune of chansons on its Parisian patio. Picking a couple of flavors (new ones are made each week) is near impossible when you have choices like pistachio, rose, violet and choco-orange. Whatever flavor you pick, pair your treat with Le Petit Beurre, Goguette’s take on the shortbread from Nantes, in the Brittany region of France. Order in advance to bring your desserts home during fall and winter — ice cream and cookies are not just for summer. 59 Montgomery Drive, Santa Rosa, goguettebread.com 

Gluten-free Carrot Cake, Zoftig Eatery

Carrot cake, done right, can be absolutely sublime. Zoftig Eatery has perfected the art of the carrot cake with a gluten-free version that has the Goldilocks ratio of just the right amount of carrot, spice, sweetness and moistness. It is rich, but not overpowering, and the cream cheese frosting is really the icing on the cake, not detracting from the flavors by being overly sweet or artificial-tasting. The secret is high-quality spices and lasting friendships: the restaurant buys the gluten-free flour for the cake from former co-owner Sonjia Spector’s childhood friend Dawn Zaft of Criminal Baking Co. We have attempted to split this generous slice of carrot cake in two and save the second half for the following day, but never succeeded. 57 Montgomery Drive, Santa Rosa, 707-521-9554, zoftigeatery.com 

Jennifer’s Picks

Gateau Parisien, Patisserie Angelica

If the words “gluten-free dessert” typically leave you cold, this ethereal treat (which won the best of show award in the 2024 Sonoma County Harvest Fair) will change your mind. Three layers of almond macaron are layered with Italian praline buttercream. It’s not overly sweet and is simply delicious. The best part? In addition to full-sized cakes, they also come in individual servings, so you don’t have to share. 6821 Laguna Park Way, Sebastopol, 707-827-7998, patisserieangelica.com

Fruit Basket Cake, Oliver’s Market

This cake perennially pops up at birthdays, retirement parties and Mother’s Day gatherings, and every single time it appears, we make a beeline for the dessert table. An eye-catching rainbow of fruit for a topping draws you in, but the layers of moist vanilla cake, pastry cream, and a hint of raspberry jam keep you coming back for just one more bite. Cakes come in 6, 8 and 10 inches, plus two sheet cake sizes for when you’re serving a crowd. Locations in Cotati, Santa Rosa and Windsor. oliversmarket.com

Peanut Butter Mousse Pie, Noble Folk

This pie is 9 inches of decadence, and it is worthy of every single, silky bite. Noble Folk’s co-owner, Christian Sullberg, fills an Oreo cookie crust with whipped peanut butter mousse and tops it all with a cloud of whipped cream. It’s a seasonal pie, usually only on the menu a couple of times a year, so keep a sharp eye out. Plus, my 2022 Thanksgiving story included a recipe for it. Super bonus! 116 Matheson St., Healdsburg, 707-395-4426; 539 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-978-3392, thenoblefolk.com

Maci’s Picks

Brownie Cupcake and Baby Fruit Galettes, Downtown Bakery & Creamery

Step into Healdsburg’s Downtown Bakery, and suddenly words like “carbs” and “calories” have no meaning. The incredibly rich and chocolaty brownie cupcake is a treat I will never pass up. And whatever fruit galette is available, get it. All of them are winners. 308 Center St., Healdsburg, 707-431-2719, downtownbakeryhealdsburg.com

Black & White Cookies, Grossman’s Noshery & Bar

A staple in New York bakeries, the black and white cookie delights with its classic chocolate and vanilla combo. Grossman’s back-and-whites are the stuff of dreams, with creamy, rich chocolate and vanilla frosting atop a soft, cake-like cookie. Not too sweet with just the right balance of flavors, it’s quite possibly the best cookie I’ve ever had. 308 Wilson St., Santa Rosa, 707-595-7707, grossmanssr.com

Apple Pecan Crumble Pie, Petaluma Pie Company

This brown sugar-sweetened apple pie is topped with a nutty crumble and a generous drizzle of housemade salted caramel for a luscious fall dessert. Bring it to the Thanksgiving table this year to switch up your traditional pie offerings and make a lasting impression. And while nothing beats grandma’s homemade, from-the-garden strawberry rhubarb pie, this humble pie shop’s sweet-tart strawberry rhubarb comes as close as it gets. 125 Petaluma Blvd. N., Suite B, Petaluma, 707-766-6743, petalumapiecompany.com

title: Bigger Kitchen, More Brunch: Wild Poppy Cafe Expands at The Barlow in Sebastopol
summary:
After building a following at their cozy west Sebastopol cafe, Martin and Danielle Maigaard have opened a larger restaurant and marketplace with sunny patio dining, brunch favorites and room to bake.

The post Bigger Kitchen, More Brunch: Wild Poppy Cafe Expands at The Barlow in Sebastopol appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
For 22 years, Martin and Danielle Maigaard dreamed of opening a restaurant with a spacious kitchen, room to bake, ample parking and an artisan marketplace bigger than a closet.

Instead, in 2024, they fell for a quirky-cool roadhouse in west Sebastopol that had none of those things. Wild Poppy Cafe, at 9890 Bodega Highway, was small, a little out of the way and simply too charming to resist.

“We wanted to start small and make sure it was received well,” Martin said.

It was. The cafe became a rarity in the restaurant business: a runaway success. Perhaps it was the quiet creekside patio, the fresh pastries or the beans and greens that became a signature dish. (This is west county, after all.)

Still, the couple dreamed of a little more space — especially in the kitchen and the parking lot.

Their new Wild Poppy Cafe and Marketplace at The Barlow delivers on both counts. Open for just a few weeks, the 3,500-square-foot former brewery has been drawing crowds for brunch and lunch, with diners settling onto the sunny patio over Korean chicken rice bowls, tacos and French toast topped with apple compote.

The Barlow is hardly short on good food and drink. Sarmentine turns out pastries, Taylor Lane serves coffee, and Acre Pizza, Sushi Kosho and Genero’s offer plenty of dining options. But Wild Poppy fills a different niche: a relaxed, brunch-friendly gathering place for Wednesday morning meetups, work-from-home days when you don’t actually want to work from home, and leisurely weekend meals.

“You walk in and it feels like home,” Martin said. “We wanted it to feel like we were hosting, like a backyard gathering or a dinner party.”

Danielle was quick to add another ingredient to the formula.

“And everyone we hire has to be nice. Customers see that, and I think that’s really helped us along.”

A new location, a familiar menu

Opening a second restaurant was no walk in the park. It was more like six months of welding torches and saws.

Martin, who has spent years renovating homes, handled much of the construction himself at the original cafe on Bodega Highway. At The Barlow, he took the same do-it-yourself approach, working without a contractor. The project took longer than expected, but the savings made the extra effort worthwhile.

The new cafe retains customer favorites, including Baja fish tacos and Cosmic Queso nachos, while adding a handful of dishes: fancy toast, salads, a salmon burger and rice bowls.

The marketplace brings together local products and fair-trade goods, including pottery, spices, blankets, napkins, towels and Wild Poppy merchandise. A deli case is being stocked with grab-and-go soups, dips and salads.

Coffee and espresso drinks share the menu with beer, wine and a sunny turmeric lemonade made in-house. Save room for the housemade gluten-free peanut butter chocolate chip cookies.

Restaurant success stories have become harder to come by. But the Maigaards appear to have found a formula that works in west Sonoma County.

That’s something worth raising a mimosa to.

Details: Wild Poppy Cafe & Market is at 6780 McKinley St., Suite 160, Sebastopol. Open 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Wednesday through Monday and closed Tuesday.

Wild Poppy Creekside is at 9890 Bodega Highway, Sebastopol. Open 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Thursday through Sunday. thewildpoppycafe.com

title: We Had Breakfast With Sonoma County’s Smashburger King
summary:
Smashburger maestro Justin Haley and dining editor Heather Irwin meet for breakfast, talking about food, life, love and favorite restaurants.

The post We Had Breakfast With Sonoma County’s Smashburger King appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Justin Haley is Sonoma County’s king of smashburgers. Not all kings wear crowns. Some wear T-shirts and chef’s pants.

You’ll usually find Haley, a gentle giant, working the flattop beneath a black pop-up tent at breweries, farmers markets and local events, turning out the thin burgers he’s perfected over the years, with crunchy cheese and char around the edges. But the real draw is the neon-orange sauce that squeezes out from every crevice.

It’s not quite Thousand Island dressing, and it’s not quite barbecue sauce. Rich with spices and a hint of smoke, it’s something entirely its own. Haley won’t tell you the recipe, but he will tell you the inspiration.

“I wanted something alarmingly orange colored,” he said. “My goal was the Nickelodeon orange. But with no dyes. I wanted that nostalgic color. And it needed to pair well with wine and beer — we’re in Sonoma County after all.”

Haley also loves working the register and holding court with customers. Children are particularly fascinated by the sauce’s improbable hue, and he often goes home with their drawings.

He’s equally generous with his fellow food vendors, sharing spare napkins, giving away burgers and lending an extra set of hands when someone is in the weeds, even during a heated food competition. He usually wins anyway. That’s just the kind of guy Haley is.

After a busy weekend of events and another People’s Choice Award, this time at the Smash Bash smashburger showdown at Shady Oak Barrel House, we met for breakfast at one of his favorite spots, Marvin’s of Cotati, to talk burgers, breakfast and the pleasures of cooking in Sonoma County.

Let’s meet for breakfast

Even on a Tuesday morning, Marvin’s is packed. Tucked into a quiet strip mall, it’s the kind of place you might drive past without a second thought. Locals know better.

The restaurant is a destination for hearty steak and eggs, pancakes and its specialty, chilaquiles: crisp tortilla chips piled with eggs, chorizo and a deep-brown mole, a smoky, slightly sweet chile sauce made in-house.

Over two generous plates of chilaquiles that threaten to overpower both our appetite and our resolve, Haley and I dig in.

First off, where did the name Thanks for the Invite come from?

My wife, Paige, and I spent months traveling across California looking for the perfect burger. We tried everything. Big cities, small towns, roadside stops. We paid attention and started to notice what made certain burgers stand out and why others were easy to forget. It was not about doing the most. It was about doing it right.

We practiced a lot back home, trying to get our own burger just right, and then invited friends over to try them. Everyone loved them and ended up saying, “Thanks for the invite!”

Why did you pick Marvin’s for our breakfast?

It’s a classic breakfast staple. They aren’t trying to do anything crazy. From the jams and jellies to salsa and mole, everything is made in-house by the family, something you don’t see much anymore.

What does breakfast look like for you on a normal day?

I don’t eat breakfast. It’s rare, but when I do, I like to kinda go all out and order pancakes to share for the table. Every time.

What’s better: Tacos or burritos?

I love them both, but I’m a nacho guy at heart. When I was 11 years old, I used to write nacho reviews. The old Rafa’s in Cotati used to bake enchilada sauce into their chips and cheese, and I think about that pretty often.

What’s something you love about cooking in Sonoma County?

The people! I feel like Sonoma County’s food community is actually massive. Whenever I have a weird idea, I know there’s always somebody nearby who’s going to try it. I feel like the community supports locals so much, something you can’t really find in a big city.

What are you obsessed with right now, food or otherwise?

Salads. I don’t look like it, but I’m a sucker for a salad. Also, my wife, Paige.

What’s your favorite restaurant or chef in Sonoma County?

Diavola. They just do everything so absolutely right, and at a price point you can’t beat. I’m a huge fan of sharing plates, and I think that’s just a perfect spot to do it. Also, the Gun Club (same owners) has our favorite smashburger (besides our own).

What would you eat for your last meal? Because I think this Mexican hot chocolate from Marvin’s is on my list.

I’d love some toasted sourdough bread, butter with a little extra salt, a little local honey, and some ripe peaches and pluots under a tree in a field in Sonoma County with the love of my life.

What food trends do you hate?

Height on food. Like, I don’t want a tall sandwich or tall burger. Flatten that thing out and make it wider. My mouth can’t open that much!

Who should I interview next?

Beryl Adler of Acorn Cafe in Healdsburg. That guy is magic, and he’s a massive inspiration.

Details about where to find Justin and Thanks for the Invite can be found at instagram.com/thanksfortheinvite.ca.
